questions.prompt: Why can't most jobs use pure deliberate practice in the same way as elite sport or music?
choices: Because work has delayed, noisy, and mixed feedback conditions
Because jobs never involve skill development
Because workers should avoid all repetition

explanation.gentle: The chapter says most jobs are too messy for the clean gold-standard loop.
explanation.direct: Professional work usually lacks stable reps, fast signals, and clear scoring.
explanation.competitive: The terrain is too dirty for a clean drill fantasy.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main workaround for workplace messiness?
choices: Ignore feedback and trust experience
Shrink the target to trainable subskills
Treat the whole profession as one repeated drill

explanation.gentle: The chapter moves from whole jobs to smaller repeatable parts of jobs.
explanation.direct: Subskill isolation is the practical bridge between workplace mess and useful practice.
explanation.competitive: If the whole blur cannot be trained, cut the blur smaller.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter say workplace feedback often has to be designed?
choices: Because natural job outcomes are often delayed or confounded
Because all managers refuse to give feedback
Because feedback only matters in schools

explanation.gentle: Job results often arrive too late or with too many mixed causes to teach clearly by themselves.
explanation.direct: Designed loops are needed because raw workplace outcomes are usually too muddy.
explanation.competitive: If the job will not hand you a sharp verdict, you have to build one.

questions.prompt: In Sonia's sales scenario, what best fits the chapter's advice?
choices: Wait for quarterly revenue totals to explain every problem
Review one call opening as a trainable subskill
Stop tracking performance entirely

explanation.gentle: She improves the loop by reviewing a smaller part of the job directly.
explanation.direct: The call opening is specific enough to inspect and correct in ways revenue totals are not.
explanation.competitive: She stops asking the scoreboard to explain the blur and corners one leaking move instead.

questions.prompt: What is Derek doing in the seminar-room teaching example?
choices: Turning vague class confusion into one reviewable explanation problem
Proving that teaching cannot improve at all
Replacing all classroom judgment with a single metric

explanation.gentle: He reduces a broad feeling to one part of the class that can be improved.
explanation.direct: The chapter favors isolating a teaching subskill instead of judging the whole class in one blur.
explanation.competitive: He puts one weak explanation sequence on trial instead of blaming the room.

questions.prompt: What danger does the chapter see in ordinary busyness at work?
choices: Busyness can hide the same recurring weakness for years
Busyness automatically lowers intelligence
Busyness prevents any experience from helping

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that activity can continue without real correction.
explanation.direct: Routine and time served can preserve a flaw if the weak part never becomes visible.
explanation.competitive: A full calendar can still be a shelter for the same old leak.

questions.prompt: Why does self-diagnosis matter more in workplace adaptation?
choices: Because private reflection is always enough by itself
Because many professionals lack constant live coaching
Because workplace feedback should replace evidence

explanation.gentle: Workers often need sharper self-review because no coach is standing beside them all day.
explanation.direct: Self-diagnosis matters when external correction is thin, but it still needs evidence and structure.
explanation.competitive: If no coach is coming, the flaw needs a sharper witness from inside the job.

questions.prompt: Which claim would the chapter reject?
choices: Workplace improvement is a partial translation of deliberate-practice logic
Messy professions can still isolate some trainable moves
A professional job automatically becomes pure deliberate practice once review starts

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps saying translation is real but partial.
explanation.direct: Starting review does not magically turn a noisy job into a clean gold-standard field.
explanation.competitive: A review log is not a magic portal to a tennis court.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's best advice for designing stronger workplace practice?
choices: Add more hours first and inspect structure later
Choose a trainable slice, build a sharper loop, and compare repeated situations
Avoid all outside feedback to preserve authenticity

explanation.gentle: The chapter emphasizes smaller targets, better loops, and stronger evidence.
explanation.direct: Practice on the job improves when professionals isolate one move and build feedback around it.
explanation.competitive: Corner the move, sharpen the verdict, and make the next rep answer.

questions.prompt: What question does this chapter hand to the next one?
choices: How can everyday life borrow some of this logic when structure is even thinner?
Why should workers stop trying to improve at all?
How can every personal habit be scored like a tournament?

explanation.gentle: The next chapter asks what survives when the setting becomes even less formal than work.
explanation.direct: The bridge moves from professional adaptation to everyday-life adaptation.
explanation.competitive: Once work has been treated honestly, the next problem is what survives even farther from structure.
